video_title: ALERT: 2027 Will Be A "Disaster" For Both Stocks & Bonds | Michael Pento
gist: Michael Pento says his model moved from net long to neutral, arguing Fed hikes pricking the debt-fueled AI bubble, a fracturing bond market and widening high-yield spreads make 2027 a likely disaster for both stocks and bonds. He prefers 1-3 year Treasuries and shorts and expects a muted flight to long bonds.

insights.claim: Pento moved his portfolio from net long (held since 2023) to net neutral in early October, as he did in December 2021; he is not yet net short. Longs (energy, aerospace and defense, healthcare, ~5% physical gold) are offset by shorts, plus T-bills and 1-3 year Treasuries.
insights.speaker: Michael Pento
insights.so_what: A systematic bull of 3+ years de-risking is a signal; positioning is hedged rather than outright bearish.

insights.claim: He admits staying bearish too long in 2022-23: he did not factor in the draining of the reverse repo facility and was wrong for the first half of 2023.
insights.speaker: Michael Pento
insights.so_what: Liquidity drains/injections can override a valuation-based bearish call for quarters.

insights.claim: He expects 2027 to be very difficult for both stocks and bonds across all durations, with only a small chance it is not a disaster; he says this holds regardless of the midterms.
insights.speaker: Michael Pento
insights.so_what: Plans for a 2022-style (or worse) simultaneous stock/bond drawdown; 60/40 portfolios are exposed.
insights.quote: There's a small chance that 2027 won't be a disaster, but it's very likely that it's going to be a disaster.

insights.claim: Risk/reward no longer favors an aggressively long buy-and-hold 60/40 portfolio; he sees 2027 as potentially very damaging for it.
insights.speaker: Michael Pento
insights.so_what: Diversification between stocks and long bonds may fail when both reprice together.

themes.theme: Fed raising rates to prick AI bubble

insights.claim: Price level is being pushed up by three things: the war in Iran, tariffs, and a debt-based monetary system with a debt-fueled AI spending spree. Rate hikes only address the third, so the Fed's only lever is to hike enough to prick the AI investment bubble.
insights.speaker: Michael Pento
insights.so_what: Fed tightening is aimed at the one inflation source it can touch, making AI-linked assets the transmission target.

insights.claim: He claims AI investment accounts for about 50% of GDP growth and 80% of earnings growth, so it will take multiple hikes to affect it, while hikes hit the bottom four income quintiles via credit card, mortgage and auto loan payments.
insights.speaker: Michael Pento
insights.so_what: Earnings and growth are concentrated in one debt-funded theme; a financing shock hits both profits and consumers.
insights.quote: 50% of all GDP growth and 80% of all earnings growth has been based on this AI investment.

insights.claim: The Fed's balance sheet grew about $200B in the last five months of Powell's tenure, but only roughly $15-20B since Warsh took office (May 22), meaning the Fed is no longer absorbing Treasury supply.
insights.speaker: Michael Pento
insights.so_what: Less Fed buying leaves the private market to price US solvency and inflation, pushing yields up.

insights.claim: Warsh is expected to take a hard line on Congress and not be the enabler of deficits and to let the market bite before easing; Taggart relays that former Kansas City Fed CEO Thomas Hoenig, who knows Warsh, agrees.
insights.speaker: Michael Pento / Adam Taggart
insights.so_what: The Fed put is further out of the money than consensus assumes; the cave point is later.

insights.claim: The bond market is fracturing: the Fed raises short rates while the long end comes under secular pressure from inflation above target for six years, insolvency, foreign creditors reducing Treasury ownership (citing confiscations and sanctions), shrinking global trade surpluses to recycle, and Bank of Japan Treasury sales.
insights.speaker: Michael Pento
insights.so_what: Long-duration Treasuries lose their traditional buyers just as supply rises.

insights.claim: The yen carry trade is dissolving: German Bunds (about 3.5%) and Japanese 10-year yields (over 3%) were near 0% from 2015-2022, so borrowing in yen to buy Treasuries, after hedging costs, no longer pays.
insights.speaker: Michael Pento
insights.so_what: Removal of a key marginal Treasury buyer and global anchor of low yields.

insights.claim: He cites US debt at 720% of revenue (versus 123% of GDP) as the right insolvency measure, arguing you cannot tax your way out because a Laffer-style curve limits revenue.
insights.speaker: Michael Pento
insights.so_what: Debt/revenue framing makes the solvency problem look far worse than debt/GDP.

insights.claim: Trillions in AI hyperscaler debt issuance are crowding out Treasuries for limited fixed-income capital.
insights.speaker: Adam Taggart / Michael Pento
insights.so_what: AI financing competes directly with government debt, lifting yields.

insights.claim: The two-year note at about 4.8% already prices roughly three rate hikes; he prefers 1-3 year Treasuries and expects the Fed eventually to cut to 1-2%, and says now is too early to lock in long yields.
insights.speaker: Michael Pento
insights.so_what: Opportunity is in the short end; the 'cure for high yields is high yields' bond-buying argument is premature to him.

insights.claim: In the next recession he expects only a short-lived, muted Pavlovian flight into long bonds, because automatic stabilizers could push the deficit from about $2T to $6T (versus a surplus in 2000 and about $1.2-1.4T peak in the GFC), with debt at $40T and 123% of GDP.
insights.speaker: Michael Pento
insights.so_what: The long bond may no longer be a recession hedge; deficit-driven supply overwhelms safe-haven demand.

insights.claim: High-yield spreads are widening sharply while Treasury yields rise, which he finds unusual and disturbing: normally spreads blow out as Treasury yields fall on flight to safety. Here, borrowing costs rising is itself widening spreads.
insights.speaker: Michael Pento
insights.so_what: No Treasury safe haven offset; credit stress is rate-driven, a worse configuration.

insights.claim: Market breadth is poor: a bit above 70% of S&P 500 stocks are in a 10%+ correction, 60% are down 20%+ and 40% are down 30%+ from 52-week highs, while the index is only 1-2% off its high.
insights.speaker: Michael Pento
insights.so_what: Headline index masks a bear market in most components.

insights.claim: Equity market cap is about 235% of GDP versus a normal 90-100%, and home prices are at record highs relative to incomes. He expects credit, housing and stocks all to unwind, with a 30% home price drop and a crash risking a depression.
insights.speaker: Michael Pento
insights.so_what: Financialization means an equity crash is systemic, forcing a policy response.

insights.claim: He currently sits in sector 4 (inflation and growth both accelerating), normally the most-long sector, but is ignoring that playbook as he expects the bond fracture to move the model to sector 2 and then sector 1 (deflation), likening it to 2007 when surging oil crushed the economy.
insights.speaker: Michael Pento
insights.so_what: Regime-based playbook with a deliberate override based on bond/credit signals.

insights.claim: In sector 1 his holdings are cash, T-bills, US dollar assets, a little gold and shorts (the four horsemen). He now holds CTAs and two short ETFs offsetting longs.
insights.speaker: Michael Pento
insights.so_what: Deflationary liquidity crises favor cash and shorts.

insights.claim: He sold his gold miners and may cut gold further: in a liquidity crisis like fall 2008 everything, including gold and levered gold stocks, is sold; gold is best when real rates are negative and falling, but real rates have spiked. He is surprised gold has not been hit harder.
insights.speaker: Michael Pento
insights.so_what: Precious metals are not a safe haven in the initial deflationary liquidity phase.

insights.claim: He trimmed his model from 20 points to 12 points to remove redundancy, and tracks credit spreads and financial conditions (now tightening) as early signals.
insights.speaker: Michael Pento
insights.so_what: Credit spreads and financial conditions are the leading inputs.

insights.claim: After a deflationary bust, he expects 'hyper stagflation': little real growth but heavy inflation as the Fed must monetize trillions annually to keep banks functioning; the Fed caves only when banks close, money markets freeze and repo rates spike, as in 2007-09.
insights.speaker: Michael Pento
insights.so_what: Long-run inflation hedges matter after the initial crash; the Fed reaction function is delayed, not absent.

insights.claim: The CRB index is up about 50% year over year, which he says will feed through the economy with a lag, not just energy.
insights.speaker: Michael Pento
insights.so_what: Commodity inflation pass-through is still ahead.

insights.claim: He would go long again if the Fed stops hiking within two quarters, i.e. Trump ends the Iran war and energy prices fall quickly, or if AI capex yields a major productivity boom.
insights.speaker: Michael Pento
insights.so_what: Defines the main upside risk to his bearish view.
insights.quote: I could be wrong and if I'm wrong I'll change my you know I'll go go long again.

insights.claim: A crack in the CRB index, oil and the five-year forward breakeven inflation rate would not be an all-clear but a signal of a recession or depression.
insights.speaker: Michael Pento
insights.so_what: Falling commodity prices would signal deflationary danger, not relief.
